text: This one lake holds more water than all five Great Lakes put together.
How does it beat all five, if it's barely bigger than Belgium?
Meet Lake Baikal in Siberia.
The Great Lakes are not impressed.
We're almost eight times bigger.
On a map? Sure.
So where is Baikal hiding all that water?
Straight down.
Bicall plunges 1,642 meters, about four times deeper than Lake Superior.
Nobody asked you to measure.
That's nearly five Eiffel Towers deep.
But why so deep?
Bicall isn't sitting in a valley.
It's filling a crack in the earth.
Right here, the ground is slowly pulling apart.
That crack opened 25 to 30 million years ago, which makes by call the oldest lake on earth.
The Great Lakes?
They filled up about 14,000 years ago.
Can we change the topic?
And the crack is still opening, about 4 millimeters every year.
Width makes the lake look big.
Depth makes it big.
Here's the twist.
The water isn't even the bottom.
Below the lake floor lies up to 7 km of mud.
The crack goes down about as far as Everest is tall, and from above, it still looks barely
bigger than Belgium.
Why do I keep getting dragged into this?
This is Boogal.
